item.title: Big Idea: The Münchhausen Trilemma — Daily Learning
item.description: The Münchhausen Trilemma says every attempt to justify a belief ends in an infinite regress of reasons, a circle in which the conclusion supports itself, or an arbitrary stopping point where you declare something true without proof. The honest move is to name your starting points, your priors, and let evidence move them when they fail.
item.content:encoded: The Münchhausen Trilemma says every attempt to justify a belief ends in an infinite regress of reasons, a circle in which the conclusion supports itself, or an arbitrary stopping point where you declare something true without proof. The honest move is to name your starting points, your priors, and let evidence move them when they fail.

item.title: Statistics: The Law of Large Numbers — Daily Learning
item.description: The more times you repeat something, the closer your observed average drifts toward its true long-run average. A bettor with a true 55% win rate might win only 4 of their first 10 bets, yet over 1,000 bets that rate tends to sit close to 55%, which is why casinos and sharp bettors trust volume over single outcomes.

item.title: Big Idea: The Twin Earth Thought Experiment — Daily Learning
item.description: In Hilary Putnam's 1975 paper, imagine a planet exactly like Earth, where the clear liquid everyone calls “water” is not H2O but a different chemical, XYZ, and where you and your Twin Earth double are molecule-for-molecule identical inside, with the same thoughts about “water” in your heads before anyone knew the chemistry in 1750. Putnam argued you still are not referring to the same thing,…
item.content:encoded: In Hilary Putnam's 1975 paper, imagine a planet exactly like Earth, where the clear liquid everyone calls “water” is not H2O but a different chemical, XYZ, and where you and your Twin Earth double are molecule-for-molecule identical inside, with the same thoughts about “water” in your heads before anyone knew the chemistry in 1750. Putnam argued you still are not referring to the same thing, because your “water” picks out H2O and theirs picks out XYZ, so meaning is not just in the head, and that raises whether a mind, or a machine trained only on text, could ever mean what we mean.

item.title: Statistics: The Lindley Paradox — Daily Learning
item.description: Flip a coin 100,000 times and get 50,400 heads, and the test calls the result significant at p ≈ 0.01 even though the rate is only 50.4%. A Bayesian reading of those same flips says they fit a fair coin far better than any specific biased alternative, so with samples that large a p-value alone can mislead you.
